flow.say: Now a cold night for glass C. Watch the water just under the ice. Tell me everything you see. Where is the brown water going?
flow.kid: Put two ice cubes gently on glass C. Watch from the side for 3 minutes.

ask.q: What did you see under the ice?
good: Thin brown streams fell down.
Brown water went through the clear water.
Brown water began to collect at the bottom.

flow.parent: Thin streams of brown water should start to fall within a minute. They are easier to see against white paper.
flow.context: In this step of Warm on Top you put ice on one glass, like a cold night over a lake. You watch what the water under the ice does.

flow.do: Ten minutes after the ice went in, compare the three glasses from the side. Your child points to the brown water in each glass. They say if it is at the top only, part of the way down, or at the bottom.
flow.say: Look at all three. In which glass is there brown water at the bottom? Tell me what you see, not what you expected.
flow.kid: After ten minutes, look at all three glasses. Point to where the brown water is in each.
flow.context: In this step of Warm on Top you compare the three glasses after ten minutes. You draw where the brown water is.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they guessed, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you guessed, what you saw, and why you think it happened. In a deep lake, fresh oxygen comes in at the top. In a hot month, can it reach the fish at the bottom? When can it?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed, what you saw, and why. When can oxygen reach the bottom of a deep lake?

ask.q: Why did the brown water sink only under the ice?
good: The ice made it cold.
Cold water is heavier than warm water, so it sank.
It became colder than the water below it.

ask.q: Why could the wind not mix glass B?
good: The warm water is light and stays on top.
Wind only stirred the top layer.

flow.parent: In most homes glass A keeps its two layers, with the line a little blurred. Glass B has ripples and a stirred top layer, but the clear water below stays clear. In glass C, brown water reaches the bottom. Write down what you really saw. The reason: warm water is lighter than cool water, so it floats. Wind pushes the top about, but cannot easily push light water down under heavy water. Ice cools the brown water until it is colder, and so heavier, than the water below. Then it sinks. A deep lake works the same way. In hot months the warm top layer hardly mixes with the cold deep water, so little new oxygen reaches the bottom. When the weather cools, the top water cools and sinks, and the lake mixes. The glass leaves two things out. A very strong wind can mix a shallow lake. And water is heaviest at 4 degrees, so near freezing it behaves differently.
flow.think: Glass C has brown water at the top and the bottom. What would have to happen for the whole glass to become one even colour?
flow.context: This is the last step of Warm on Top. You explain why only cooling sent the top water down, and what that means for a deep lake.

activities.title: One River, Three Homes: map the Kaveri from the hills to the sea
activities.context: In this activity you draw the Kaveri river from its source to the sea. You mark its three stretches, and work out who lives in each one and why. You will find out why one river has very different homes along its way.

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper, the bigger the better
a pencil and blue, green and brown colours
an atlas or a phone map of South India (helpful, not needed)

activities.record: A side-on map of the Kaveri in three stretches, with at least two living beings named or drawn in each stretch and one reason written beside each.

example_chart.title: The Kaveri in three stretches
rows: Cold, clear, fast and shaded by forest
Leaves that fall in from the trees
Insect young under stones, small hill-stream fish, frogs
Wider, with rocky pools and sunlit shallows
Algae on the stones, insects and smaller fish
Humpback mahseer, smooth-coated otters, mugger crocodiles
Slow, deep and turbid, split into many branches
Fine bits from upstream, and plankton
Carp, catfish, egrets and herons, and mangroves at the sea's edge

setup.art: A child drawing a long blue river across a sheet of paper from green hills on the left to the sea on the right.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the river from the hills to the sea.

setup.art: The same drawing divided by two pencil lines into three parts labelled upper, middle and lower.
setup.caption: 2. Divide it into three stretches. Write what the water is like in each.

setup.art: The finished map with small drawings of insects and leaves in the hills, a big fish and an otter in the middle, and birds and mangroves at the delta.
setup.caption: 3. Write or draw who lives in each stretch, and write one reason.

flow.do: Before drawing, ask your child how a river changes between the hills and the sea. Write down what they say.
flow.say: Think of a river high in the hills and the same river near the sea. What is different about the water? Would the same animals live in both places? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Picture a river in the hills and the same river near the sea. How is the water different?

ask.q: What changes along a river?
good: It gets wider and slower.
The water gets muddier.
It is cold at the top and warm lower down.

flow.parent: Accept every idea for now. The table comes in step 3.
flow.context: This is the first step of One River, Three Homes. You say how you think a river changes from the hills to the sea.

flow.do: Your child draws the Kaveri across the page. On the left are the hills of Kodagu, with the source at Talakaveri. In the middle the river passes Srirangapatna and the falls at Hogenakkal. On the right the river splits into branches in the delta and meets the Bay of Bengal. Add two tributaries, the Kabini and the Bhavani, and one dam at Mettur.
flow.say: Start thin in the hills and get wider as you go. Tributaries join from the sides. At the delta the river splits into many branches. Now divide your river into three stretches: upper, middle and lower.
flow.kid: Draw the Kaveri from the hills to the sea. Or lay a string on the floor. Add two tributaries and one dam. Divide the river into three stretches.
flow.parent: The map need not be accurate. What matters is the order: hills, rocky middle, flat delta, sea.
flow.context: In this step of One River, Three Homes you draw the Kaveri from Talakaveri to the Bay of Bengal and divide it into three stretches.

flow.do: Read the table out, one row at a time. For each stretch, your child writes what the water is like and names two who live there. Ask why each one fits that stretch.
flow.say: In the hills the stream is shaded, so few algae grow. What could the small animals there eat? In the middle the Sun reaches the stones. What grows on them? Near the sea the water is slow and muddy. Who can find food where it is hard to see?
flow.kid: Write what the water is like in each stretch. Name two who live there, or draw them. Say why each one fits.

ask.q: Why does the mahseer live in the middle stretch and not in the delta?
good: She needs clean, flowing water with rocks.
The delta water is slow and muddy.
Her food lives among the stones.

check.q: What is the main food in a shaded hill stream?
options: Leaves that fall in from the trees
Algae growing on the sunny stones
Plankton drifting in slow water
check.why: A shaded stream gets little light, so few algae grow. The food comes from the forest, as fallen leaves. If you chose algae or plankton, think about where those need to live: in sunlight, and in slow water.

flow.context: In this step of One River, Three Homes you fill in who lives in each stretch of the river, and why.

flow.do: Point to the dam on the map. Ask what changes below the dam and above it. Then ask what reaches the sea.
flow.say: Look at your dam. Silt settles in the still lake behind it. What does the delta get less of? A fish wants to swim from the delta up to the hills. What happens? Now look at the river's mouth. What does the river give to the sea?
flow.kid: Look at your dam. What does it stop? What does the river carry to the sea?

ask.q: What does a river give to the sea?
good: Fresh water.
Silt that builds the delta.
Plant food for the plankton of the coast.

flow.parent: Good answers name silt, fish and flow. The dam also gives stored water for crops. Both sides are in the explanation card 'Should a river be dammed?'
flow.context: This is the last step of One River, Three Homes. You work out what a dam changes, and what the river gives to the sea.

activities.title: The Squeeze Test: feel the water press on your hand
activities.context: In this activity you push your hand, inside a thin plastic bag, down into a bucket of water. You feel how the water presses, and where it presses hardest. You will find out what a deep-sea animal has to live with.

materials.item: a bucket of water, at least 25 centimetres deep
a clean thin plastic bag, big enough for a hand and wrist, with no holes
a pencil and paper

activities.record: A drawing of the hand in the bag under water, with arrows showing where the bag pressed. Longer arrows mean a harder press. Or tell your grown-up, who writes down where it pressed hardest.

example_chart.title: How hard sea water presses at different depths
rows: A diver on a coral reef
The bottom of the sunlit zone
A sea cucumber on the abyss floor

setup.art: A child's hand inside a loose clear plastic bag held above a bucket of water.
setup.caption: 1. Put your hand in the bag. Keep the open end above the water.

setup.art: The same hand pushed deep into the bucket, the bag now clinging tightly to every finger while the open end stays above the surface.
setup.caption: 2. Push your hand slowly to the bottom. Feel the bag.

flow.do: Your child puts one hand into the bag. Ask what they think the bag will do under water, and why.
flow.say: Your hand is in a loose bag full of air. You will push it down into the water, with the top of the bag kept out. What will the bag do? Will it feel the same at your fingertips and at your wrist? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put your hand in the bag. Think about how it will feel under water.

ask.q: What do you expect to feel?
good: The bag will stick to my hand.
It will squeeze more lower down.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Squeeze Test. You guess what a plastic bag will do to your hand under water.

flow.do: Your child pushes the hand slowly down, fingers first, until the fingertips touch the bottom. The open end of the bag stays above the water. Ask them to notice the bag at the fingertips and at the wrist. Then they turn the hand palm up, palm down and sideways.
flow.say: Go down slowly. What is the bag doing? Where is it tightest? Now turn your hand over. Does the water press only from above, or from every side?
flow.kid: Push your hand slowly to the bottom. Then turn your hand palm up, palm down and sideways.

ask.q: Where did the water press hardest?
good: At my fingertips, which were deepest.
It pressed from every side, not only from above.

flow.parent: The air is pushed up and out of the bag, and the plastic clings to the skin. The cling is firmest at the deepest point.
flow.context: In this step of the Squeeze Test you push your bagged hand to the bottom of the bucket. You feel where the water presses hardest.

flow.do: Your child points with a finger to every place where the bag pressed. Then read the table of depths together. After your child has said what they noticed, read them the note below.
flow.say: You felt the press of about 25 centimetres of water. Look at the table. At 10 metres the press is double the press at the surface. What happens at 4,000 metres? Why are the animals there not crushed?
flow.kid: Point to every place the bag pressed your hand. Then read the table together.

ask.q: Why is a deep-sea fish not crushed?
good: Her body is mostly water, and water cannot be squeezed much.
She has no air spaces inside.
The press is the same inside and outside.

check.q: In which direction does water press on a fish?
options: From every side
Only from above
Only from below
check.why: Water presses on every part of a surface, from every direction. You felt this when the bag clung all round your hand. If you chose 'only from above', think of how the bag pressed on your palm even when it faced down.

flow.parent: The air in the bag was pushed out because air can be squeezed and moved easily. Water hardly squeezes at all. A deep-sea animal has no air-filled spaces, so there is nothing in her to crush.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Squeeze Test. You draw how the water pressed on your hand, and read how hard the deep sea presses.

activities.title: Red Turns Black: why many deep-sea animals are red
activities.context: In this activity you look at red, blue, black and white paper under blue light in a dark room. You find out why a red animal is hard to see in the deep sea.

materials.item: small pieces of red, blue, black and white paper, or crayon patches of these colours on white paper
a phone that can show a plain blue screen
a room that can be made dark

activities.record: A small table: the colour of each paper in room light, and the colour it seemed to be in blue light.

setup.art: Four small squares of paper, red, blue, black and white, lying in a row on a table in normal light.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out red, blue, black and white paper.

setup.art: A dark room with a phone showing a plain bright blue screen held above the four squares, the red and black squares both looking black.
setup.caption: 2. Make the room dark. Shine a plain blue screen on the papers.

flow.do: Lay the four papers in a row. Tell your child that only blue light reaches the twilight zone of the sea. Ask what each paper will look like in blue light.
flow.say: Deep in the sea the only light left is blue. Here are four colours. What will each one look like when only blue light shines on it? Which will be easiest to see, and which hardest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Only blue light reaches the deep sea. Look at the four papers and think about each one.

ask.q: What will the red paper look like?
good: Purple, because red and blue mix.
Dark, because there is no red light to bounce off it.

flow.parent: Many children expect purple. Let the test decide.
flow.context: This is the first step of Red Turns Black. You guess what four colours of paper will look like in blue light.

flow.do: A grown-up finds a plain blue picture on the phone and shows it full screen at full brightness. Switch off the lights and close the curtains. Hold the screen about 10 centimetres above the papers.
flow.say: Look at the four papers now. What colour does each one seem to be? Which two look almost the same?
flow.kid: Make the room dark. Shine the blue screen on the papers. Which two look almost the same?

ask.q: What did you notice?
good: The red paper looks black or very dark.
Red and black look almost the same.
White looks blue.

flow.parent: A phone's blue is not perfectly pure, so the red paper may look very dark brown and not fully black. A torch covered with blue cellophane also works.
flow.context: In this step of Red Turns Black you shine blue light on four colours of paper in a dark room.

flow.do: Switch the lights on. Your child fills in the table and says what they found. After they have answered, read them the note below.
flow.say: Say what you guessed and what you saw. Many prawns and jellyfish of the deep sea are bright red. Is that a good colour for hiding there? Why?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Say what you guessed and what you saw.

ask.q: Why is red a hiding colour in the deep sea?
good: No red light reaches there.
A red body sends back no light, so it looks black.

check.q: Why does a red prawn look black in the deep sea?
options: No red light reaches her to bounce back
Her colour washes off in deep water
The pressure changes her skin
check.why: A red thing looks red because it sends back red light and soaks up the rest. Deep water has no red light left, so nothing comes back. If you chose another answer, remember the red paper: it did not change, only the light did.

flow.parent: A red surface sends back red light and soaks up the other colours. Sea water soaks up red light near the top, and blue travels deepest. In blue light a red animal sends back almost nothing, so she looks black. The same prawn looks bright red in a net at the surface.
flow.context: This is the last step of Red Turns Black. You explain why a red body is hard to see where the only light is blue.

activities.title: The Falling Meal: how much food reaches the deep sea floor?
activities.context: In this activity 100 grains of rice stand for the food made in the sunlit sea. You move them down through the zones, and count how many reach the bottom.

materials.item: grains of raw rice, counted out
a sheet of paper and a pencil
small bowls or katoris for the eaten grains

activities.record: A table with three rows, one for each zone: grains that arrived, grains eaten there, grains that sank on.

example_chart.title: The Falling Meal: 100 grains from the top to the floor (rounded from real measurements)

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three pencil lines across it making four bands labelled sunlit zone, twilight zone, midnight zone and sea floor.
setup.caption: 1. Draw four bands down the page: three zones and the sea floor.

setup.art: A heap of 100 rice grains in the top band and a child's finger sliding a small group of grains down into the second band.
setup.caption: 2. Start with 100 grains at the top. Most are eaten in each zone. Slide the rest down.

setup.art: The page at the end, with three small bowls of rice beside the bands and only two grains lying in the bottom band.
setup.caption: 3. Count the grains that reach the sea floor.

flow.do: Draw three lines across the paper to make four bands. Label them from the top: sunlit zone, twilight zone, midnight zone and sea floor. Put all 100 grains in the top band. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: These 100 grains are all the food that plankton make in the sunlit sea. No food is made below. Some of it sinks. How many of the 100 grains do you think will reach the sea floor, 4,000 metres down? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: 100 grains of food are made at the top. How many will reach the sea floor? Why?

ask.q: What might happen to the food on the way down?
good: Animals eat it.
Bacteria rot it.
It takes a long time to sink.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Falling Meal. You guess how much of the food made at the top of the sea reaches the bottom.

flow.do: Read the table one row at a time. In the sunlit zone your child moves 80 grains into a bowl, as eaten, and slides 20 down. In the twilight zone 17 are eaten and 3 slide down. In the midnight zone 1 is eaten and 2 slide to the floor.
flow.say: In the sunlit zone, animals and bacteria eat 80 of the 100 grains. Only 20 sink out. Count them. Sinking food is called marine snow. In the twilight zone 17 of those are eaten. How many are left to sink on? What happens in the midnight zone?
flow.kid: Move the eaten grains into a bowl at each zone. Slide the rest down. How many reach the floor?
flow.parent: The numbers are rounded from measurements with traps hung in the sea. They differ from sea to sea and from season to season. The real share reaching the deep floor is about 1 to 3 in 100.
flow.context: In this step of the Falling Meal you move rice grains down through the zones of the sea. At each zone most of the grains are eaten.

flow.do: Compare the bowl from the sunlit zone with the 2 grains on the floor. Ask what this means for the animals of the deep.
flow.say: Look at the bowl from the top and the 2 grains at the bottom. If you lived on the sea floor, how would you live? Would there be many of you or few? Would you be fast or slow?
flow.kid: Compare the top bowl with the two grains at the bottom. Is there more food or less food down here?

ask.q: What does so little food mean for deep-sea animals?
good: There are few of them, spread far apart.
They move slowly to save energy.
They must not miss a meal.

check.q: Where is most of the food of the deep sea floor made?
options: In the sunlit zone, far above
In the mud of the sea floor
In the dark water just above the floor
check.why: Food is made where there is light. It then sinks as marine snow, and most is eaten on the way. If you chose the mud or the dark water, remember that nothing there can catch sunlight. Only at vents do bacteria make food in the dark.

flow.context: In this step of the Falling Meal you compare the food at the top of the sea with the food that reaches the floor.

flow.do: Ask what would happen at the bottom if the top made less food. Then ask about the time the fall takes.
flow.say: Suppose the plankton at the top make only half as much food one year. What happens on the floor? A flake sinks about 100 metres in a day. How long does a flake take to fall 4,000 metres?
flow.kid: The top makes half as much food. What happens at the bottom?

ask.q: How long does marine snow take to fall 4,000 metres?
good: About 40 days, because 4,000 divided by 100 is 40.

flow.parent: Half the food at the top means about 1 grain at the bottom. Deep-sea animals feel a poor year at the surface a few weeks later.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Falling Meal. You work out what happens on the sea floor when the surface makes less food.

activities.title: Echo Ears: find a wall with your eyes shut
activities.context: In this activity you shut your eyes and make a steady 'shhh' sound. From the sound alone, you tell whether a steel plate is held in front of your face. Then you try it with noise in the room. You will find out how a river dolphin can find fish in muddy water.

materials.item: a steel plate, a tray or a large hardbound book
a cloth for a blindfold (closing the eyes also works)
a noisy fan, a running tap or music for the second round
paper and pencil to keep score

activities.record: Two scores out of 10: right answers in a quiet room, and right answers in a noisy room.

setup.art: A blindfolded child making a 'shhh' sound while a parent holds a steel plate about a hand's width in front of the child's face.
setup.caption: 1. Eyes shut. Say 'shhh' without stopping. Is the plate there or not?

setup.art: The same game with a table fan whirring loudly beside them and the child looking unsure.
setup.caption: 2. Try again with noise in the room. Is it harder?

flow.do: Tell your child that a river dolphin finds things by sound. Ask whether they think a person could notice a plate by sound alone, and why.
flow.say: A river dolphin clicks and listens for the echo. You will make a 'shhh' sound with your eyes shut. I will hold a plate in front of your face, or take it away. Do you think you will be able to tell? Why?
flow.kid: A plate is held in front of your face. Can sound alone tell you? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Echo Ears. You guess whether you can notice a steel plate using only sound.

flow.do: Your child shuts their eyes and says a long steady 'shhh'. First let them practise: move the plate slowly towards their face and away, about 10 centimetres at the nearest. Then play 10 turns. On each turn, silently hold the plate there or keep it away. Your child says 'plate' or 'no plate'. Keep score.
flow.say: Keep the 'shhh' going. Listen to how it changes as the plate comes close. Now the test. Ten turns. Tell me each time: plate or no plate?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Say a long 'shhh'. Listen to it change. Then say 'plate' or 'no plate' ten times.

ask.q: How did the sound change when the plate was near?
good: It got louder.
It sounded closer and sharper.
It sounded hollow.

flow.parent: Move the plate without making a breeze or a sound. Most children score 8 or more out of 10 after a little practice.
flow.context: In this step of Echo Ears you shut your eyes and say 'shhh'. You tell from the sound whether a plate is in front of your face.

flow.do: Switch on a noisy fan, a tap or some music, and play 10 more turns. Compare the two scores. After your child has said what they noticed, read them the note below.
flow.say: Now the room is noisy. Ten more turns. Was it harder? A river dolphin depends on echoes to find food and to keep clear of nets. What might the noise of boat engines do to her?
flow.kid: Play ten more turns with noise in the room. Count how many you get right.

ask.q: Why was it harder in a noisy room?
good: The noise covered the echo.
I could not hear the small change in the sound.

check.q: Why does a Ganga river dolphin use sound to find fish?
options: Light cannot pass far through muddy water
Fish in the Ganga are very noisy
Sound cannot travel through clear water
check.why: Her river is turbid, so eyes are of little use there. Sound travels well through muddy water. If you chose 'sound cannot travel through clear water', that is not so: sound travels well through all water.

flow.parent: The 'shhh' bounces off the plate and returns to the ears, so it sounds louder and nearer. That is a small form of echolocation. A dolphin's clicks are much sharper and her hearing far finer than ours. Engine noise covers her echoes, as the fan covered yours.
flow.context: This is the last step of Echo Ears. You try the game in a noisy room and think about boat noise in a dolphin's river.

projects.title: My Water File: one lake, tank or river near my home
projects.context: In this four-day project you find out about one water body near your home. You find where its water comes from, who lives there and what is changing it.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper, folded and stapled into a small file
a pencil and colours
a phone map, with a grown-up
the white disc and thread from the Vanishing Disc Test (if you can visit the water)

projects.safety: Go near water only with a grown-up. Stay on steps, a bridge or a firm bank. Do not go into the water, and wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Choose a lake, tank or river. Find it on a map. Find where its water comes from and where it goes.
Visit with a grown-up if you can, or phone an older person who knows the place. Note the colour, the clearness, the plants and the birds.
List six living beings of the place. Draw who eats what, and mark the food that comes from outside.
Write what is changing the place. Present your file to the family.

projects.record: A four-page file. Page 1: a map with the water's way in and way out. Page 2: what you saw or were told. Page 3: six living beings and their food. Page 4: what is changing the place, and one question you still have.

setup.art: A child and a parent looking at a phone map showing a blue lake in a city, with a hand-made paper file open beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: find your lake, tank or river on a map. Where does its water come from?

setup.art: A child standing with a grown-up on the stone steps of a tank, lowering a white disc on a thread and writing in a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: visit with a grown-up, or phone someone who knows the place.

setup.art: A notebook page with six small drawings of a heron, a fish, a frog, a lotus, a dragonfly and green water, joined by arrows.
setup.caption: 3. Day 3: lay out six living beings and who eats what.

setup.art: A child holding up a small paper file and talking to two family members on a sofa.
setup.caption: 4. Day 4: write what is changing the place, and present your file.

flow.do: Help your child choose the nearest lake, tank, pond or river, and find it on a phone map. Follow the blue lines on the map to see what flows in and what flows out. Your child draws a simple map on page 1.
flow.say: Which water is nearest to us? Let us find it on the map. Where does its water come from: rain, a stream, a canal or a drain? Where does the water go when the place is full?
flow.kid: Choose a lake, tank or river near you. Find it on a map. Draw where its water comes from and goes, or trace it from the map.

ask.q: Where does this water come from?
good: From rain running off the streets.
From a canal that comes from a river.
From a stream in the hills.

flow.parent: Every city has one. Chennai has Pallikaranai marsh and Chembarambakkam lake. Bengaluru has Ulsoor and Hebbal lakes. Hyderabad has Hussain Sagar. Kochi has the backwaters. If the map does not show the inflow, ask a neighbour who has lived there long.
flow.context: This is day 1 of My Water File. You choose a lake, tank or river near your home and find where its water comes from.

flow.do: If you can visit, go together in daylight and stay on steps or a firm bank. Your child notes the colour and smell of the water, the plants at the edge and any birds. From steps or a bridge, they can lower the white disc and measure the depth at which it vanishes. If you cannot visit, phone an older person who knows the place. Ask what it was like 30 years ago.
flow.say: What colour is the water? Can you see the bottom at the edge? Which plants grow in the shallow part? Which birds are here, and what are they doing? Write down what you see. Do not write what you expect.
flow.kid: Visit with a grown-up, or phone someone who knows the place. Write the colour, the plants and the birds.

ask.q: What does the colour of the water tell you?
good: Green means many algae.
Brown means mud is washing in.
Clear means few bits are floating in it.

flow.parent: Good questions for an older person: Could you see the bottom then? Which fish were caught? Did the place dry up in summer? What flowed in?
flow.context: This is day 2 of My Water File. You visit the water with a grown-up, or ask an older person about it, and write what you find.

flow.do: On page 3 your child writes six living beings of the place on small slips of paper, from yesterday's notes. They lay the slips on the floor so that each food sits next to the one who eats it. They stick them on the page, or take a photo. Then they circle any food that comes from outside the water.
flow.say: Who lives here? Who eats whom? Now think of this lesson. Does any of the food come from outside the water: leaves from trees on the bank, insects from the land, waste from a drain?
flow.kid: Write six living beings of your place on slips. Lay each food next to who eats it. Circle the food that comes from outside.

ask.q: What food comes into the water from outside?
good: Leaves that fall in.
Insects that land on the water.
Plant food washed in by rain or drains.

flow.parent: Algae and green water count as living beings. So do the birds, even though they fly off at night.
flow.context: This is day 3 of My Water File. You draw who lives in your lake, tank or river, and where their food comes from.

flow.do: On page 4 your child writes what is changing the place: building on the edges, drains, rubbish, less water or new plants. They add one question they still have. Then they present the file to the family in three minutes.
flow.say: What has changed here since your grandparents were young? What is the biggest change? Tell us about your place in three minutes. End with the one thing you most want to find out.
flow.kid: Write what is changing your place. Add one question you still have. Present your file in three minutes.

ask.q: What must people look after to keep this place healthy?
good: The streams and drains that flow in.
The land around the edge.
The way out, so that the water can keep moving.

flow.parent: Praise a clear reason more than a neat page. The last question links the project to the main idea of the unit: a water home is fed from outside its edges.
flow.context: This is day 4 of My Water File. You write what is changing your lake, tank or river, and present the file.

challenges.title: Bring Up the Deep: collect bottom water without mixing in the top
challenges.context: In this challenge a jar holds brown salty water at the bottom and clear water on top. You build a tool that brings up a sample of the brown bottom water, as scientists do from the deep sea. You will find out how to take water from the deep without mixing in the top.
challenges.problem: Scientists need water from 4,000 metres down, to measure its oxygen and its salt. On the way up, the sample must not mix with any of the water above. Your deep sea is a tall jar. The bottom 3 centimetres are brown salty water, and the rest is clear. Bring up a sample of the brown water that is still brown.
constraints: Your fingers must not go below the surface of the water.
The sample must be at least 10 drops.
Dropped on a white plate, the sample must be clearly darker than a drop taken from the top of the jar.
You may not stir, tilt or pour the jar.
materials: a tall clear jar, or a 2-litre plastic bottle with the top cut off by a grown-up
half a cup of strong black tea with 2 tablespoons of salt dissolved in it, cooled
a very small bottle or a pen cap, some thread and a little clay or atta dough
a medicine dropper or a syringe without a needle, if you have one
a white plate and a teaspoon
general: Hold a finger over the top of a straw and lower it to the bottom. The air inside keeps the clear water out. Lift the finger, so that brown water enters. Press the finger down again and lift the straw out.
Tie a thread to a small weighted bottle with a loose plug of dough. Lower it to the bottom. Pull a second thread to take the plug out, wait for the bottle to fill, and lift it slowly.
Push a straw onto the end of a syringe or dropper. Lower the straw to the bottom and draw the water up.
creative: Join two straws to reach deeper, and seal the join with tape so that no air leaks in.
Give the small bottle two threads, one to pull the plug out and one to push a second plug in, so that it comes up closed.
Lower a bit of sponge on a thread inside a straw, let it soak at the bottom, and pull it up through the straw.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own sampler. Draw it first, or describe it to your grown-up, and mark what keeps the top water out on the way down and on the way up. Build it, test it and drop the sample on the white plate. Then change one thing to make the sample darker.

setup.art: A tall clear jar with a dark brown layer of water at the bottom and clear water above, standing on a table beside a white plate.
setup.caption: 1. The jar: brown salty water at the bottom, clear water on top.

setup.art: A child lowering a drinking straw into the jar with one finger pressed over the top end of the straw.
setup.caption: 2. Build a tool that reaches the bottom. Keep your fingers out of the water.

setup.art: Two drops on a white plate side by side, one pale and one dark brown, with a child pointing at the dark one.
setup.caption: 3. Drop your sample on a white plate beside a drop from the top. Is it darker?

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the bottle, if you use one. Pour the salty tea into the jar, about 3 centimetres deep. Hold a tablespoon just above the tea. Pour tap water very slowly onto the spoon, until the jar is nearly full. Read the problem together.
flow.say: The brown water is your deep sea. It is salty, so it is heavy and stays at the bottom. You must bring some up without mixing it with the clear water. How could you do that? Tell me three ideas before you build.
flow.kid: The brown water at the bottom is your deep sea. How can you bring some up, still brown? List three ideas.

ask.q: What is the hard part of this problem?
good: The tool passes through the clear water on the way down.
The sample could leak or mix on the way up.

flow.parent: If the layers mix while you pour, the water went in too fast. Start again and pour more slowly.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bring Up the Deep. You make a jar with brown water at the bottom and think of ways to bring a sample up.

flow.do: Your child builds a sampler from the materials. Help to hold things, but let your child decide the design. Put a drop from the top of the jar on the white plate, for comparing later.
flow.say: Build your first idea. Before you test it, tell me two things. What keeps the clear water out on the way down? What keeps the brown water in on the way up?
flow.kid: Build your sampler. What keeps clear water out on the way down? What keeps brown water in?
flow.context: In this step of Bring Up the Deep you build a tool to collect water from the bottom of the jar.

flow.do: Your child lowers the sampler slowly, takes a sample and lifts it out. They drop the sample on the white plate, beside the drop from the top. Compare the two colours.
flow.say: Go down slowly, so that you do not stir the jar. Take your sample and bring it up. Put it on the plate. Is it darker than the drop from the top? Is it as dark as the bottom layer looks?
flow.kid: Lower your sampler slowly. Take a sample. Drop it on the plate. Is it darker than the top drop?

ask.q: If the sample is pale, where did the clear water get in?
good: On the way down, before the tool reached the bottom.
The tool was not right at the bottom when it opened.
It leaked on the way up.

check.q: A straw is lowered with a finger pressed on top. Why does no water enter?
options: The air trapped inside keeps the water out
The straw is too thin for water
Water cannot move upwards
check.why: With the top closed, the air inside has nowhere to go, so water cannot push in. Lift the finger and the air escapes, and water enters from the bottom. If you chose 'too thin', try the straw with the top open.

flow.context: In this step of Bring Up the Deep you test your sampler. You compare your sample with a drop from the top of the jar.

flow.do: Your child changes one thing and tests again. Then compare the design with real deep-sea samplers, using the note below.
flow.say: What went wrong, or what could be better? Change one thing and test again. Real samplers go down open and are shut at the right depth. How do you think someone on a ship shuts a bottle 4,000 metres below?
flow.kid: Change one thing to get a darker sample. Test again.

ask.q: How could a bottle be shut from far above?
good: Send a weight sliding down the cable to hit a catch.
Send an electric signal down a wire.
Use a timer.

flow.parent: Praise a clear account of what went wrong as much as a dark sample. Ocean scientists lower a ring of open tubes on a long cable. At each chosen depth one tube is snapped shut, by a signal from the ship or by a weight sent down the cable. Each tube then holds water from one depth only.
flow.context: This is the last step of Bring Up the Deep. You improve your sampler, and compare it with the bottles that scientists lower into the sea.

challenges.title: A Way Round the Wall: build a fish pass
challenges.context: In this challenge a tilted tray stands for a river with a wall across it. You build a row of small pools that lets water down gently, so that a fish could swim up.
challenges.problem: A barrage has been built across a river. The water above the wall is 6 centimetres higher than the water below. Hilsa are coming up from the sea to lay their eggs, and they are not strong jumpers. Build a way round the wall, made of small steps and resting pools, that a fish could climb.
constraints: The pass must go from the low end of the tray to the high end, 6 centimetres up.
No step between two pools may be higher than 1 centimetre.
Every pool must hold water at least 1 centimetre deep after the pouring stops.
When one tumbler of water is poured in slowly at the top, it must pass through every pool.
Use only clay or dough, foil, pebbles and the tray.
materials: a tray or a baking tin, about 30 centimetres long
books to raise one end of the tray 6 centimetres
clay, plasticine or stiff atta dough, about two handfuls
kitchen foil, about half a metre
a steel tumbler of water and a ruler
a towel, because this is wet work
general: Make a foil gutter along the tray. Build low walls of dough across it, like steps, so that a pool forms behind each wall.
Cut a small notch in the top of each wall, so that the water flows through one place and not over the whole wall.
Make more steps than you think you need. Six centimetres needs at least six steps of 1 centimetre.
creative: Bend the gutter into a zigzag, so that it is longer and each step can be lower.
Put the notches on opposite sides of each wall in turn, so that the water winds and slows down.
Lay pebbles in the pools, so that a fish has still water to rest behind.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own fish pass. Draw it from the side first, or describe it to your grown-up, and write the height of each step. Build it and pour the water. Measure every step and every pool. Then change one thing to make the flow gentler.

setup.art: A baking tray raised on books at one end, with a ruler standing beside the high end showing 6 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Raise one end of the tray 6 centimetres.

setup.art: A foil gutter running along the tilted tray with six low dough walls across it, each wall with a small notch.
setup.caption: 2. Build a row of pools with low walls. No step higher than 1 centimetre.

setup.art: Water being poured from a steel tumbler into the top pool and trickling from pool to pool down the gutter while a child measures a step with a ruler.
setup.caption: 3. Pour water in at the top. Does it pass through every pool?

flow.do: Raise one end of the tray on books until it is 6 centimetres higher than the other end. Read the problem together. Ask for ideas before any building.
flow.say: The top of the tray is the river above the wall. The bottom is the river below. A fish must get up, and she cannot jump high. What could you build? How many steps will you need if each is 1 centimetre?
flow.kid: A fish must climb 6 centimetres. She cannot jump more than 1 centimetre. What will you build?

ask.q: How many steps of 1 centimetre are needed to climb 6 centimetres?
good: At least six.
More than six, if some steps are lower.

flow.context: This is the first step of A Way Round the Wall. You set up a tilted tray and plan a fish pass of small steps and pools.

flow.do: Your child lines a channel with foil and builds dough walls across it. Help to press the dough down firmly, so that water does not leak underneath. Let your child decide where the walls go.
flow.say: Build your pools. Press each wall down hard at the bottom and the sides. Where will the water leave each pool? Check each step with the ruler as you go.
flow.kid: Build your pools with dough walls. Press them down well. Measure each step with the ruler.
flow.parent: Dough walls need to be about a finger thick. Water finds every gap, so the first test nearly always leaks. That is part of the challenge.
flow.context: In this step of A Way Round the Wall you build a row of small pools up a tilted tray, with dough walls and foil.

flow.do: Your child pours one tumbler of water slowly into the top pool. Watch where the water goes. When it stops flowing, measure the depth of each pool and the height of each step.
flow.say: Pour slowly and watch. Does the water go through every pool, or does it find a short cut? Now measure. Is any step higher than 1 centimetre? Is any pool too shallow to rest in?
flow.kid: Pour water in at the top. Does it pass through every pool? Measure each step and each pool.

ask.q: Where would a fish have trouble in your pass?
good: At the step that is too high.
Where the water rushes fast through a narrow gap.
In the pool that is too shallow.

check.q: Why does a fish pass have pools between the steps?
options: So the fish can rest in slower water
So the pass uses more water
So the pass looks like a staircase
check.why: Swimming up against fast water is hard work. A pool is deeper and slower, so a fish can rest there before the next step. If you chose 'looks like a staircase', remember that fish do not walk: each step is a short climb through flowing water.

flow.context: In this step of A Way Round the Wall you pour water down your fish pass. You measure every step and every pool.

flow.do: Your child changes one thing to fix the worst step or pool, and tests again. Then compare the design with real fish passes, using the note below.
flow.say: Which step or pool was the worst? Change one thing and test again. Your pass suits a fish who can climb 1 centimetre. Would the same pass suit every kind of fish in the river?
flow.kid: Fix the worst step or pool. Test again.

ask.q: Why might one fish pass not suit every fish?
good: Some fish jump and some do not.
Big fish need deep pools.
Some fish swim near the bottom and some near the top.

flow.parent: Praise a clear account of what went wrong as much as a working pass. Real fish passes are of several kinds: rows of pools, long winding side channels like small streams, and lifts that carry fish up in a tank of water. Passes built for strong jumpers have often failed for other fish. A pass has to be designed for the fish of that river, and tested with them.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Way Round the Wall. You improve your fish pass, and compare it with the passes built at real dams.

worksheets.title: Life in water: the main ideas

items.p: Which of these is a freshwater habitat?
items.why: A tank holds rain or river water with very little salt. A coral reef, the deep sea floor and a salt pan all have salty water.

items.p: Why do plants and algae grow only in the top layer of a lake or sea?
opts: Only that layer has enough light
The deep water is too clean
Fish eat all the deep plants
items.why: Plants and algae make food from light. Water takes light away with depth, so below the sunlit zone no food can be made.

items.p: What does a river drop when its water slows down?
items.why: Slow water cannot carry sand and silt, so they settle. This builds floodplains and deltas.

items.p: What is marine snow?
opts: Dead plankton and waste sinking through the sea
Ice that falls on the sea in winter
Salt that settles on the sea floor
White sand washed in by rivers
items.why: Marine snow is dead plankton, droppings, slime and dust stuck together. It is the main food of the deep sea.

items.p: The flat land beside a river that goes under water in a flood is the ____.
a: floodplain
items.why: A floodplain is covered when the river spills over its banks. The flood leaves silt there.

items.p: Finding things by making a sound and listening for the echo is called ____.
a: echolocation
items.why: River dolphins and many bats use echolocation where eyes are of little use.

items.p: Light fades faster in muddy water than in clear water.
items.why: True. Bits of mud bounce light away in all directions, so less light gets through each layer.

items.p: Nothing lives in the sea below 1,000 metres.
items.why: False. Animals live at every depth. A fish has been filmed at 8,336 metres.

items.p: Match each ocean zone to its depth.
items.why: The zones are set by light and depth. Enough light for photosynthesis ends at about 200 metres, and all sunlight ends at about 1,000 metres.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one still water or flowing water?
items: a lake
Still water
a village tank
Still water
a marsh
Still water
a hill stream
Flowing water
a river
Flowing water
a spring
Flowing water
items.why: In still water, tiny drifting beings can stay in one place. In flowing water, living beings must hold on or swim against the current.

items.p: Put these in order, as a river flows from source to sea.
items: A spring in forested hills
A fast, cold, shaded stream
A wide river with rocky pools
A slow, deep, muddy river
A delta with many branches
a: A spring in forested hills
A fast, cold, shaded stream
A wide river with rocky pools
A slow, deep, muddy river
A delta with many branches
items.why: A river starts small, steep and fast. It grows wider, slower and muddier, and drops its sediment at the mouth.

items.p: A hill stream is shaded and has few algae. What do the small animals there eat?
items.a: They eat dead leaves that fall into the stream from the trees. Insect young shred the leaves, and small fish eat the insects.
items.why: A strong answer says that the food comes from outside the stream, from the forest.

items.p: Why is a deep-sea fish not crushed by the water above her?
items.a: Her body is mostly water, and water can hardly be squeezed. She has no air-filled spaces. The pressure is the same inside her and outside.
items.why: A strong answer says that pressure crushes gas-filled things, and that the fish has none.

items.p: Draw a lake from the side. Show where plants grow, where plankton drift and where it is dark.
items.a: A lake in side view. Rooted plants stand at the shallow edge. Dots of plankton are in the bright top water. The deep middle is shaded dark, with no plants.
items.why: A strong drawing puts every food maker in the light: rooted plants where the bottom is shallow, and plankton near the surface.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: A new dam is planned on a river where fish swim upstream to breed.

views.says: Build it. Stored water will give us a second crop in the dry months.

views.who: A fisher at the river mouth
views.says: Do not build it. The fish will not reach their breeding places, and our catch will go.
Build it only with a fish pass that suits these fish, and let water through all year.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from the unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that hilsa above the Farakka Barrage almost vanished after 1975. Another is that most rain falls in four months, so stored water matters. A strong answer also says what the other view gets right.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses what a dam gives and what it stops: water for crops, and fish, silt and floods.

worksheets.title: Life in water: light, layers and rivers

items.p: A disc vanishes at 12 centimetres in cloudy water. The cloudiness is doubled. About where does the disc vanish now?
items.why: Twice as many bits take the light away in about half the distance. If you chose 24, you doubled the depth, but more bits mean a smaller depth.

items.p: In a deep lake in a hot month, where is there least oxygen?
opts: Among the plants at the edge
items.why: Oxygen comes in at the top. The warm layer hardly mixes with the cold layer below, where bacteria keep using oxygen up.

items.p: Which living being fits a slow, deep, muddy river best?
opts: A dolphin who finds fish by echoes
A fish who hunts by sight
A lotus rooted in the river bed
An insect who clings to clean stones
items.why: In muddy water sight is of little use, and the deep dark bed grows few plants. Sound works well there.

items.p: A strong wind can easily push warm top water down under cold water.
items.why: False. Warm water is lighter and floats. Wind stirs the top layer, but the layers mix only when the top cools.

items.p: River water that reaches the sea still does useful work.
items.why: True. It carries silt that builds the delta, pushes back salt water, and feeds the plankton of the coast.

items.p: Match each living being to the clue that fits their home.
pairs: A sucker belly for holding on to rock
Clicks and echoes in muddy water
Long stalks from mud up to the light
A glowing lure in the dark
items.why: Each body answers the main problem of its home: fast water, muddy water, deep still water, airless mud or darkness.

items.p: Sort these. Is the food made inside this habitat, or brought in from outside?
items: algae on sunny river stones
Made inside
plankton in a lake's top water
Made inside
bacteria's food at a hot vent
Made inside
fallen leaves in a shaded stream
Brought in from outside
marine snow on the abyss floor
Brought in from outside
silt and plant food in a delta
Brought in from outside
items.why: Food is made inside only where there is light, or chemical energy at a vent. Dark and shaded waters are fed from elsewhere.

items.p: Three of these are harmed by a wall across a river. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Silt on its way to the delta
Paddy fields fed by a canal
items.why: A dam or barrage sends water into canals, so the fields gain. The fish, the silt and the dolphins are stopped by the wall.

items.p: Marine snow sinks 100 metres a day. How many days does it take to fall 3,000 metres?
items.why: 30 days. 3,000 divided by 100 is 30.

items.p: Put these in order, from the cool season to the end of the hot season in a deep lake.
items: The whole lake is mixed and rich in oxygen
The Sun warms the top water
A warm layer floats on a cold layer
Bacteria use up oxygen in the cold layer
Fish leave the deep water
a: The whole lake is mixed and rich in oxygen
The Sun warms the top water
A warm layer floats on a cold layer
Bacteria use up oxygen in the cold layer
Fish leave the deep water
items.why: Layers form because warm water floats. Once the layers stop mixing, the deep water gets no new oxygen.

items.p: A tank turns muddy after building work nearby. What happens to the plants on the bottom, and why?
items.a: The mud makes the water turbid, so light fades in a shorter distance. Plants on the deeper parts of the bottom no longer get enough light to make food, and die back. Only plants in the shallowest water remain.
items.why: A strong answer links turbid water to less light, and less light to less photosynthesis.

items.p: No rain falls on a delta village, yet the river rises and turns red-brown. Explain how.
items.a: Rain fell far upstream, days earlier. It washed soil into streams, and the streams joined the river. The flood and its silt travelled down the river to the delta.
items.why: A strong answer says that a river gathers water and sediment from all the land it drains, and carries them a long way.

items.p: Why do fish farmers stir their ponds on hot, still nights?
items.a: Warm water holds less oxygen, and at night no algae are making any. With no wind, little oxygen comes in from the air. Stirring brings water to the surface, where it takes up oxygen.
items.why: A strong answer names the surface as the place where oxygen enters, and says that stirring brings deep water there.

items.p: A city marsh is full of birds. The city wants to fill part of it to build houses.

views.who: A family waiting for a house
views.says: People need homes near their work. The marsh is only wet waste land.
In heavy rain the marsh holds the flood water. Fill it, and the streets will flood.
More than a hundred kinds of birds feed here. They have nowhere else in the city.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from the unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that a wetland takes in flood water and feeds many living beings. Another is that people do need homes. A strong answer suggests where else the houses could go, or how much of the marsh must stay.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer shows what the marsh does, and takes the families' need seriously.

items.p: Draw a river from hills to sea. Label the source, a tributary, the floodplain, the delta and the mouth.
a: Source: where the river begins, high in the hills
Tributary: a smaller river that joins the main river
Floodplain: flat land beside the river that floods
Delta: flat land built of sediment where the river splits
Mouth: where the river meets the sea
items.why: A strong answer puts the parts in the right order, and shows the river growing wider towards the sea.
items.art: A blank box for the child's own drawing of a river, with five empty label lines beside it.

worksheets.title: Life in water: think it through

items.p: Each 10 centimetres of a pond lets half the light through. How much is left at 30 centimetres?
items.why: Half is left at 10 centimetres, a quarter at 20 and an eighth at 30. If you chose 'none', remember that halving never quite reaches zero.

items.p: Vent bacteria make food without light. What do vent animals still need that was made in sunlight?
opts: Oxygen dissolved in the sea water
items.why: The bacteria and animals at vents use oxygen. That oxygen was made by algae and plants in the light, and carried down by sinking cold water.

items.p: A dam lets out water from the bottom of a deep reservoir. What is that water like in a hot month?
opts: The same as the surface water
items.why: In hot months the deep layer is cold and has lost oxygen. Fish below the dam then meet water that is colder and poorer in oxygen than the river was.

items.p: Why are many animals of the twilight zone see-through or red?
opts: Both colours are hard to see there
Red and clear bodies need less food
items.why: In open water there is nothing to hide behind. A clear body lets the faint light pass. A red body sends back no light, because no red light reaches that depth.

items.p: A foam cup shrinks in the deep sea because foam is full of tiny pockets of air.
items.why: True. Air can be squeezed into a smaller space. Water can hardly be squeezed, so a water-filled body keeps its shape.

items.p: A fair test of cloudy water can change the milk and the lighting together.
items.why: False. If two things change, you cannot tell which one caused the result. Only the milk should change.

items.p: Pressure rises by 1 kilogram on each square centimetre for every 10 metres. How much at 2,500 metres?
items.why: 250 kilograms. 2,500 divided by 10 is 250. Add about 1 kilogram for the air above the sea.

items.p: Of every 100 parts of surface food, 2 reach the sea floor. How many of 1,000 parts?
items.why: 20 parts. 1,000 is 10 times 100, and 10 times 2 is 20.

items.p: Bacteria at hot vents make food from the energy in chemicals. This is called ____.
a: chemosynthesis
items.why: Chemosynthesis means making food with chemical energy. Photosynthesis means making food with light.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last in the story of a meal on the abyss floor.
items: Phytoplankton make food in the sunlit zone
The plankton die and clump into flakes
The flakes sink for several weeks
Most flakes are eaten on the way down
A sea cucumber eats what reaches the mud
a: Phytoplankton make food in the sunlit zone
The plankton die and clump into flakes
The flakes sink for several weeks
Most flakes are eaten on the way down
A sea cucumber eats what reaches the mud
items.why: Deep-sea food begins in the light and travels down. Only about 1 to 3 parts in 100 arrive.

items.p: A scientist dredged one sea and said no life exists below 550 metres anywhere. What was wrong with his reasoning?
items.a: He stretched a result from one sea to all seas. The sea he sampled happens to be poor in life. He also had no samples from very deep water, so he was guessing beyond his evidence.
items.why: A strong answer says that a result holds only for what was tested, and that more places and greater depths had to be sampled.

items.p: A lake's Secchi depth was 3 metres ten years ago and is 1 metre now. Give two possible causes.
items.a: More mud may be washing in, from building or bare land around the lake. Or more algae may be growing, fed by sewage or farm fertiliser. Both make the water turbid.
items.why: A strong answer names things that put more bits into the water. It may add how to tell them apart: mud makes water brown, and algae make it green.

items.p: Is the deep sea floor a habitat that looks after itself? Give evidence for your answer.
items.a: No. Almost no food is made there. Its food sinks from the sunlit zone as marine snow, and its oxygen is carried down from the surface. Only at vents is food made in the dark, and even there the oxygen comes from above.
items.why: A strong answer uses the Falling Meal, and says where the food and the oxygen come from.

items.p: Metal-rich lumps lie on the deep sea floor. Some countries want to collect them for making batteries.

views.says: These metals are needed for clean energy. Mining the sea floor harms no forest and no village.
We have seen very little of that floor. Animals there grow slowly, and may never recover.
Explore and study first. Decide about mining when we know who lives there.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from the unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that deep-sea animals get very little food, so they grow and recover slowly. Another is that the metals are needed, and mining on land also does harm. A strong answer says what should be found out first.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses what the unit says about the slow life of the deep sea, and about how little has been seen.

items.p: Draw three glasses with warm brown water on top: still, windy and iced. Show where the brown water goes.
items.a: The still glass has a brown layer on top and clear water below. The windy glass has ripples and the same two layers. The iced glass has thin brown streams falling and brown water at the bottom.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that only cooling sent the top water down. Wind stirred the top layer only.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

quiz.p: Which pair are both freshwater habitats?
opts: A lagoon and a coral reef
A salt pan and a tank
quiz.why: Lakes and rivers hold water with very little salt. Reefs, salt pans and the abyss are salty.

quiz.p: About what share of all the kinds of fish live in fresh water?
quiz.why: About half of all kinds of fish live in fresh water. Rivers and lakes are cut off from each other, so each grows kinds of its own.

quiz.p: What happens to light as it goes deeper into water?
opts: It gets weaker with every layer
It stays the same to the bottom
quiz.why: Each layer of water soaks up and scatters a share of the light. If you chose 'turns red', remember that red is the first colour to be lost.

quiz.p: Where in a deep lake do rooted plants such as lotus grow?
opts: Floating far from shore with no roots
quiz.why: A rooted plant needs a bottom shallow enough for light to reach, or for the stalk to reach the surface.

quiz.p: Why does warm water stay on top of cold water in a lake?
opts: Wind holds the warm water up
Fish push the cold water down
quiz.why: Warm water is a little lighter than cold water, so it floats. That is why the two layers hardly mix in hot months.

quiz.p: What makes a layered lake mix from top to bottom?
opts: The top water cools and sinks
The Sun heats the top water more
quiz.why: When the top water cools, it becomes as heavy as the water below and sinks. Then wind can mix the whole lake.

quiz.p: Which stretch of a river is cold, clear, fast and rich in oxygen?
opts: The upper stretch, near the source
The lower stretch, near the sea
quiz.why: Near the source the stream is steep and tumbles over rocks, which stirs in oxygen. Shade keeps the water cold.

quiz.p: Why do many river fish lay their eggs on flooded land?
opts: The young find food and hiding places there
quiz.why: Warm shallow flood water fills with plankton and insects, and plants give cover. The young return to the river as the flood goes down.

quiz.p: How does a wall across a river harm a fish like the hilsa?
opts: She cannot reach her breeding places upstream
The wall makes the water salty
The wall takes away her gills
quiz.why: Hilsa live in the sea and breed in rivers. A wall with no suitable way round cuts the journey.

quiz.p: By how much does the pressure rise for every 10 metres of depth in the sea?
opts: By about 1 kilogram on each square centimetre
By 10 kilograms on each square centimetre
quiz.why: Every 10 metres of water adds about as much press as the whole of the air above us: about 1 kilogram on each square centimetre.

quiz.p: Where does most of the food eaten on the deep sea floor come from?
opts: It sinks from the sunlit zone
Rivers pour it straight onto the floor
Deep-sea fish make it from light
quiz.why: Food is made where there is light, and sinks as marine snow. Only about 1 to 3 parts in 100 reach the floor.

quiz.p: In a fair test of how milk hides a disc, what is the one thing that changes?
quiz.why: Only the thing you are testing should change. If the light or the observer changed too, you could not tell what caused the result.

applications: Lake scientists and volunteers lower a white disc every month. A falling Secchi depth warns them that mud or algae are building up.
Water treatment plants measure how turbid the river water is before they clean it, so that they know how much cleaning is needed.
Fish and prawn farmers run paddle wheels on hot still nights, to stir oxygen into the pond before the fish run short.
Engineers build fish passes at dams and barrages, and plan how much water to let through for the river all year.
Flood warning offices measure river levels far upstream. They work out when the flood will reach the towns and villages lower down.
Builders of deep-sea vehicles use thick metal balls and small windows, because the water presses hundreds of times harder than air.
Fishing boats and research ships find fish and map the sea floor with echo sounders, which work by sending sound and timing the echo.
Scientists who count river dolphins can listen for their clicks with underwater microphones, as well as watching for them to surface.

open_questions.q: How do hilsa in the sea sense that a river is in flood?
open_questions.why_open: They might follow the fresher water, the mud, a smell or the change in flow. Tracking small fish in a muddy sea is hard, and nobody has shown which sign matters most.

open_questions.q: How deep can a fish live?
open_questions.why_open: The deepest fish filmed was at 8,336 metres, and the sea goes down to almost 11,000. Very few dives have looked, so the true limit is not known.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of animals live in the deep sea?
open_questions.why_open: Almost every deep dive finds species that have no name yet. People have seen only a very small part of the deep sea floor.

open_questions.q: Did life on Earth begin at vents on the sea floor?
open_questions.why_open: Vents offer energy and chemicals with no sunlight. Shallow pools on land offer other things. Nobody has yet made life from chemicals in either setting.

open_questions.q: How much water must be left flowing in a river to keep the river alive?
open_questions.why_open: Fish, silt, the delta and the sea all need some flow, and the amounts differ for every river. Scientists and governments still argue about how to work it out.

Why is the sea blue in pictures, and the Godavari brown?
The fish on our plate today: was she from a river, a pond or the sea? What did she eat?
If our street floods in the rain, where does that water go next?
What would you want to look for first on a dive to the deep sea floor?
Is a river the same river if all its water is new every few weeks?

jokes.j: Why do deep-sea fish never need an umbrella?
jokes.a: Their snow is the edible kind.

jokes.j: What did the sea cucumber say about dinner?

jokes.j: Why did the river dolphin do so well at school?

jokes.j: Why was the lake so calm in summer?
jokes.a: It had sorted everything into layers.

maths.problem: In a made-up Vanishing Disc Test, the disc vanished at 24 centimetres with 1 teaspoon of milk. It vanished at 12 centimetres with 2 teaspoons, and at 6 centimetres with 4. What is the pattern? Predict the depth for 8 teaspoons and for 16.
maths.answer: Each time the milk doubles, the depth halves. With 8 teaspoons the depth would be about 3 centimetres. With 16 it would be about 1.5 centimetres.
maths.explain: 24 divided by 2 is 12, and 12 divided by 2 is 6. So doubling the milk halves the depth. Half of 6 is 3, and half of 3 is 1.5. Another way to see it: teaspoons times depth is always 24. 1 times 24, 2 times 12 and 4 times 6 are all 24.
maths.context: In the Vanishing Disc Test you lower a white disc into water with more and more milk. These made-up results follow a simple pattern.

chart.title: Made-up results: depth at which the disc vanished

maths.why_maths: A pattern lets you predict a result before you measure it. If the measurement then disagrees, you have found something worth looking into.

maths.problem: In a muddy pond, every 10 centimetres of water lets through half of the light that enters it. 100 units of light arrive at the surface. How much light is left at 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 centimetres? A water plant needs at least 10 units. How deep can she grow?
maths.answer: 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and about 3 units. The plant can grow down to about 30 centimetres, where 12.5 units are left. At 40 centimetres only 6.25 units are left, which is too little.
maths.explain: Halve the light for each 10 centimetres. Half of 100 is 50, half of 50 is 25, half of 25 is 12.5, half of 12.5 is 6.25, and half of 6.25 is about 3. The light never reaches zero, but it soon falls below what a plant needs.
maths.context: The Vanishing Disc Test shows that cloudy water takes light away quickly. This problem follows the light down through a muddy pond, layer by layer.
maths.why_maths: Halving again and again shows why light falls fast at first and then slowly. It also shows why a small rise in muddiness can leave pond plants in the dark.

maths.problem: In the sea, the press on each square centimetre rises by about 1 kilogram for every 10 metres of depth. A vehicle dives to 6,000 metres. By how much has the press on each square centimetre risen? Its window is 10 centimetres by 10 centimetres. What is the total extra press on the window?
maths.answer: The press has risen by 600 kilograms on each square centimetre. The window has 100 square centimetres, so the total extra press is 60,000 kilograms. That is 60 tonnes, about the weight of 12 elephants.
maths.explain: 6,000 divided by 10 is 600. The window's area is 10 times 10, which is 100 square centimetres. 600 times 100 is 60,000 kilograms. There are 1,000 kilograms in a tonne, so that is 60 tonnes. A large elephant weighs about 5 tonnes, and 60 divided by 5 is 12.
maths.context: In the Squeeze Test you felt 25 centimetres of water press on your hand. This problem works out the press on a small window 6,000 metres down.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the press on one square centimetre by the area shows why a deep-sea vehicle needs a very thick hull and small windows.

maths.problem: Marine snow sinks about 100 metres a day. Plankton bloom at the surface on 1 June. The sea floor is 3,700 metres down. On what date does the first of that food reach the floor?
maths.answer: On 8 July. The fall takes 37 days.
maths.explain: 3,700 divided by 100 is 37 days. June has 30 days, so 29 days after 1 June is 30 June. That leaves 8 more days, which brings us to 8 July.
maths.context: In the Falling Meal you moved rice grains from the top of the sea to the floor. This problem works out how long the real fall takes.
maths.why_maths: Working out the delay shows that the deep sea feels what happens at the surface, but weeks later.

maths.problem: About 2 parts in 100 of the food made at the surface reach the deep sea floor. Above one patch of floor, the surface makes 5,000 kilograms of food in a year. How much reaches the floor? If the surface made only 3,000 kilograms, how much would reach it?
maths.answer: 100 kilograms reach the floor. In the poorer year, 60 kilograms reach it.
maths.explain: One part in 100 of 5,000 is 50, so 2 parts are 100 kilograms. One part in 100 of 3,000 is 30, so 2 parts are 60 kilograms. The floor loses 40 kilograms of a supply that was already small.
maths.context: In the Falling Meal only 2 grains of 100 reached the sea floor. This problem uses the same share for a real patch of sea. The amounts are made up.
maths.why_maths: A share out of 100 lets you scale up from 100 grains of rice to any amount of food, and compare a good year with a poor one.

maths.problem: Heavy rain falls on hills 1,200 kilometres up a river from a delta village. Suppose the flood moves down the river at about 5 kilometres an hour, day and night. How many days later does the river rise at the village? The village had no rain that week. What would the people there see?
maths.answer: The river rises 10 days later. The people would see the river rise and turn muddy under a dry sky.
maths.explain: 1,200 divided by 5 is 240 hours. 240 divided by 24 is 10 days. The speed is made up for this problem. Real floods move at different speeds in different stretches of a river.
maths.context: In One River, Three Homes you drew a river from the hills to the sea. This problem follows a flood down a long river.
maths.why_maths: Dividing distance by speed tells you when a flood will arrive. Flood warning offices do this sum to warn villages downstream.

how_we_found_out.context: This card tells how people found out that animals live in the deep sea, and how some of them live without food from sunlight.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1841 the naturalist Edward Forbes dragged a net along the floor of the Aegean Sea. The deeper he went, the fewer animals came up. In 1843 he wrote that life in the sea probably stopped at about 550 metres. For 25 years most scientists agreed. The deep was dark, cold and under huge pressure, so the idea seemed sensible. Then Michael Sars, a professor in Norway, listed hundreds of species from deeper water off his own coast. In 1869 Charles Wyville Thomson brought up animals from 4,289 metres. Forbes had not been careless. He had sampled one sea that is poor in life, and stretched his result to every sea. A second surprise came in 1977. Scientists in the submarine Alvin found hot springs on the sea floor, crowded with giant tube worms. Nobody could say what the worms ate. In 1981 a student, Colleen Cavanaugh, showed that bacteria inside the worms make food from chemicals in the vent water.
how_we_found_out.who: Edward Forbes, Michael Sars and Charles Wyville Thomson in the 1800s. Jack Corliss and Tjeerd van Andel, who dived in Alvin in 1977. Colleen Cavanaugh, who explained the tube worms in 1981.
how_we_found_out.when: Forbes wrote in 1843. Thomson's deep dredge was in 1869. The vents were seen in February 1977, and the tube worm paper was published in 1981.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That no life exists in the sea below about 550 metres. Dredges in the 1860s brought up animals from far deeper, down to 4,289 metres in 1869. Forbes had sampled one sea that is poor in life.
how_we_found_out.art: Sailors on the deck of an old sailing ship emptying a dredge net of starfish and sea lilies onto the planks while a man in a long coat bends to look.

roots.context: In this lesson you watched light fade in cloudy water, and you followed food from the top of the sea to the bottom. Here we ask what that says about where any home ends.

deep_truth.truth: In the Vanishing Disc Test, a few spoons of milk hid the disc one hand's depth down. Light fades fast in water, so food can be made only near the top. Yet fish live at the bottom of the deepest lake and sea. They eat food that was made far above and sank to them. So most of a water home is fed from somewhere else.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a habitat as a place with edges that looks after itself: this pond, this river, the deep sea. But the deep sea eats what the surface made, and a hill stream eats leaves from the forest. A habitat's food and oxygen often come from outside its edges.
deep_truth.evidence: Only 1 to 3 parts in 100 of the food made at the sea surface reach the deep floor, and nearly all deep-sea animals live on it. Shaded hill streams are fed mostly by fallen leaves. A delta is built from the silt of hills far upstream. Even vent animals breathe oxygen made in the light.

three.who_am_i: The water in your body was in a river, a cloud and the sea before it was in you. The fish and rice on your plate grew with silt and rain from places you have never seen.
three.what_is_life: Living beings do not stay inside the edges we draw. A hilsa needs the sea and the river. A deep-sea worm needs the algae four kilometres above her.
three.what_is_this_world: The sunlit top of the water, the dark bottom, the river, the floodplain and the sea are parts of one working whole. Food, oxygen and mud keep moving between them.

roots.thread: All the water on Earth is one water, moving. It rises from the sea, falls on the hills, and runs back as rivers. On the way it becomes many homes: a stream, a tank, a flooded field, a delta, a dark sea floor. Each home looks separate, and each has its own living beings. But the Vanishing Disc Test and the Falling Meal show that they feed each other. The Chandogya Upanishad says something close to this about rivers. Once they reach the sea, they are simply the sea.

teachings.teaching: The teacher Uddalaka tells his son that the rivers of the east flow east and the rivers of the west flow west. They rise from the sea and go back to the sea, and become the sea. There, they do not know 'I am this river' or 'I am that river'.
teachings.link: This is the water cycle, seen more than 2,500 years ago. Uddalaka uses it to say that separate things share one source. In this lesson the science is plainer. The mud, the food and the fish of a river really do become part of the sea.

science.text: Deep-sea animals depend on the sunlit surface. Sediment traps show that only 1 to 3 parts in 100 of surface food reach the deep floor, and that deep-sea life rises and falls with the supply.

Some scientists think life on Earth began at vents on the sea floor, where rock, water and chemicals meet. Others think it began in shallow pools on land that dried and filled again. The evidence does not yet decide between them.

other_view.who: Stephen Forbes, an American biologist, in his talk 'The Lake as a Microcosm' (1887), and scientists who study lakes in this way
other_view.view: Forbes described a lake as a little world within itself. The fish of a lake cannot leave, and everything they need must be found inside its shores. On this view a lake does have real edges, and that is exactly why it can be studied as a whole. Seeing every habitat as open to every other can blur a difference that matters to a fish.

practice.title: One glass of water: where has it been?
practice.say: Pour a glass of drinking water and hold it in both hands. Take one slow sip. Now go backwards. Before the glass, this water was in a pipe or a can. Before that, a tank, a lake, a river or the ground. Before that it was rain, and before the rain it was the sea. Sit quietly for one minute and picture each place. Then take a second sip.
practice.kid: Hold a glass of water. Take one slow sip. Where was this water before the tap? And before that? Go back as far as the sea. Then sip again.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through carefully but not yet tried at home. The Vanishing Disc Test (core) needs a bucket, about 10 teaspoons of milk, a white bottle cap, two coins, thread and tape. The depths depend on the milk and the bucket. With a full bucket, the disc may still be seen on the bottom after 1 teaspoon. That is fine, and the step says what to write. If the disc vanishes within 3 centimetres, start again with half-teaspoons. Do the test in bright shade, because direct sunshine makes a glare. The doubling pattern is only rough at home. Warm on Top needs three clear glasses, strong tea without milk and two ice cubes. A grown-up makes the tea and cools it to bath-water warmth. The tap water in the glasses must be at room temperature, not from the fridge, or the cooled tea will not sink through it. Pour the tea slowly onto a spoon, or the layers mix. One River, Three Homes needs only paper and colours. The Squeeze Test needs a thin plastic bag with no holes. Red Turns Black needs a dark room and a phone showing a plain blue picture, which a grown-up finds. The red paper looks very dark, though perhaps not fully black. The Falling Meal needs 100 grains of rice, and its numbers are rounded. Echo Ears needs a partner and a steel plate. Whose Home Is This? and Dive to 6,000 can each be played by one child, who counts their own score. My Water File needs a grown-up for the map and for any visit to water, and can be done by phone if a visit is not possible. Bring Up the Deep needs a tall clear jar, and the salty tea must be poured in first. A Way Round the Wall is wet work, so use a tray and a towel. Dough walls usually leak on the first try. No part needs a garden, a pet or a wild animal.
